overview: This file documents U.S. occupation authorities’ evolving treatment of Japan’s postwar telephone system, especially the compulsory purchase of 36,000-yen government bonds by new subscribers and the speculative private market in transferable “telephone rights.” A September 1948 despatch questions official claims that the bond merely covered installation costs, characterizing it instead as a forced loan or revenue measure to expand the network, while an enclosed SCAP letter explains its legal and financial basis. A January 1949 despatch and its enclosures record SCAPIN 1964, which sought to suppress speculation and the resale or rental of government telephone service after February 15, 1949, release reserved equipment, impose a three-month limit on approved applications, and preserve only limited transferability for pre-existing rights.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 579 on the Japanese Telephone Bond Law
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports a change in occupation policy toward foreign residents’ purchase of compulsory Japanese telephone bonds and evaluates the bond as a revenue-raising measure.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 579: foreign residents no longer need prior consent to buy the telephone bond; the Mission argues the ¥36,000 charge functions as a forced loan rather than cost coverage, and firms would prefer higher monthly rates to the upfront cost.

subfiles.title: GHQ letter to the Eighth Army on the Telephone Bond Law
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers; signed by J. F. Bradshaw by command of General MacArthur
subfiles.about: Explains the terms, financial rationale, rates, and licensing implications of Japan’s compulsory telephone-bond system.
subfiles.summary: GHQ letter: applicants must buy a ¥36,000, 15-year, 4%-interest bond, justified by inflation eroding old fees; compulsory bond purchases by licensed firms are ruled business costs, not prohibited yen investments, with occupation personnel paying their own bonds.

subfiles.title: Partial duplicate of GHQ letter on the Telephone Bond Law
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Preserves the first page of a duplicate copy of the August 18 GHQ explanation of the telephone-bond system.
subfiles.summary: Partial duplicate repeats the GHQ letter's opening on the compulsory telephone bond and comparative Tokyo-U.S. rates, ending before the licensing interpretation and signature.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 55 on speculation in telephone rights
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards and analyzes a SCAP directive and press release intended to restrict speculation and profiteering in Japanese telephone rights and service.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 55: SCAPIN 1964 bars transferring post-February 1949 telephone rights, limits approvals to 3-month fulfillment, and bans resale, though older rights remain transferable; the bond is now framed as financing plant expansion, not reimbursing installation costs.

subfiles.title: SCAPIN 1964: Treatment of Telephone Rights and Prohibition of Resale
subfiles.from: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers; signed by R. M. Levy
subfiles.about: Directs the Japanese government to end recognition of newly transferred telephone rights, restrict applications, release facilities, and prohibit resale or rental of public telecommunications service.
subfiles.summary: SCAPIN 1964 makes post-February 1949 telephone contracts non-transferable and valueless as property, approving only quickly fillable applications, protecting reserved equipment only until April 1949, and banning resale except for simultaneous transfers of older rights or approved special services.

subfiles.title: Press release: “Direct Japanese to Abolish Private Speculation in Telephones”
subfiles.from: Public Information Office, General Headquarters, Far East Command
subfiles.about: Publicizes SCAP’s restrictions on telephone-right speculation and explains the historical development and economic effects of the private market.
subfiles.summary: Press release traces speculative telephone rights (selling up to 55,000 yen, rentals 10-12x legal rates) to old high fees; postwar reform cuts fees to 1,800 yen but requires new subscribers to buy a 36,000-yen bond, with service movable but not sellable.

interest: Shows postwar Japanese telephone bonds and transferable rights shifting from installation financing to a speculative asset market.
